title: Product Engineering Interview Briefs
summary: Twelve quick reviews for preview races, durable job correctness, role fit, and credible ownership stories.
audience: Engineers reviewing before a product engineering interview.

cards.title: Interview: Supersede
cards.prompt: A is active; B then C are submitted before A settles. What should run next?
cards.explanation: Run C after A settles, and suppress A’s obsolete result. The bounded pending slot retains only C. Starting both increases concurrency beyond the contract; keeping A as the visible answer ignores current intent. Completion order cannot determine which input the artist now wants.

cards.title: Interview: Abort
cards.prompt: The provider ignores AbortSignal and resolves after dispose. What prevents a stale render?
cards.explanation: A disposed/revision guard before every UI callback. Cancellation is a request to cooperating operations. A guard still prevents late local callbacks when cancellation is ignored; changing loading state cannot cancel an operation or prove remote work stopped.

cards.title: Interview: Error
cards.prompt: A fails after B was submitted. What should the coordinator do?
cards.explanation: Suppress A’s obsolete error and continue with B. Errors need the same revision guard as results: A no longer describes current intent. The slot must be released in finally so B can run; otherwise one old failure blocks all future work.

cards.title: Interview: Deadline
cards.prompt: The active adapter never settles. Which statement is accurate?
cards.explanation: The baseline blocks; a timeout alone does not prove remote work stopped. Finally runs when control leaves the awaited operation, not after an implicit timeout. Promise.race changes which promise you await; it does not stop the remote operation. Define deadline, cancellation, and capacity policy explicitly.

cards.title: Interview: Uncertain
cards.prompt: A provider finished an export; the worker crashed before recording success. What is the safest retry plan?
cards.explanation: Before repeating the effect, reconcile via a stable provider key or operation ID where supported. Redelivery proves the message needs handling, not that the external effect failed. Otherwise keep the uncertainty explicit; neither blind retries nor invented success preserve correctness.

cards.title: Interview: Outbox
cards.prompt: The API writes a job, then crashes before publishing its queue message. Which design closes this gap?
cards.explanation: Commit the job, credit reservation, and outbox record atomically so dispatch intent survives a crash. Publishing first can create work without an accepted job or reservation. A tab cannot preserve the backend acceptance contract.

cards.title: Interview: Idempotency
cards.prompt: Two workspaces reuse the same idempotency key. What is the correct boundary?
cards.explanation: Scope the key to the workspace and compare the request fingerprint. Tenant scope prevents unrelated requests colliding or leaking results. A body fingerprint detects changed requests under the same key. Prompt text omits workspace, input revision, model, and configuration identity.

cards.title: Interview: Fencing
cards.prompt: Worker A pauses, its lease expires, and worker B commits success. A resumes. What protects the result?
cards.explanation: A guarded state transition with the current attempt/fencing token. A lease can expire while its previous holder is still running. The commit must validate attempt ownership and state/version, so stale workers cannot overwrite B. Last-write-wins is unsafe for results and ledger transitions.

cards.title: Interview: Evidence
cards.prompt: A generic interview site lists likely company questions without candidate provenance. How should you use it?
cards.explanation: Treat these as optional, inferred practice material, not candidate evidence of the company’s actual questions. They establish neither the exact interview loop nor a contradiction with a specific briefing. Confirm logistics directly and prioritize primary role and product material.

cards.title: Interview: Role
cards.prompt: A product engineering role combines frontend and collaboration work with durable jobs. How should preparation change?
cards.explanation: Include frontend state, rendering, product judgment, and collaboration boundaries. The role spans product surfaces and reliability, so the interview preparation should connect them. Backend-only study misses explicit qualifications; syntax memorization alone cannot explain state ownership or user-visible correctness.

cards.title: Interview: Rate
cards.prompt: Your story says traffic grew from 500 to 50,000 RPM. Which statement is accurate?
cards.explanation: That is 100×, about 8.3 to 833 requests/second; define what was measured. Divide requests per minute by 60 and calculate the ratio as 50,000/500. Explain peak versus sustained, ingress versus processed events, and success rate so a capacity claim remains meaningful and defensible.

cards.title: Interview: Recovery
cards.prompt: Tests and a build pass after an incident fix. What can you honestly claim?
cards.explanation: Code validation passed. The final pruned runtime’s startup, deployment, and customer recovery each need separate evidence. Name unknown impact. Local dependencies can hide packaging failures.
